Koh Samui's main road is the 51 km ring road, Route 4169, which is mostly two lanes and takes about 90 minutes to drive round without stopping. Two connectors branch off it: Route 4170 in the south-west (Lipa Noi, Thong Krut, Taling Ngam), which is steep, narrow and slippery when wet, and Route 4171 in the north-east (Bangrak, Plai Laem, Choeng Mon and the Big Buddha). Traffic drives on the left, most crashes happen on wet hills and at night, and police run regular checkpoints near Chaweng Lake Road, the airport and along the ring road, where the helmet fine is up to 2,000 THB per person.

Good to know: laws and fines on this page were checked in November 2026 and are general information, not legal advice. Road numbers follow the standard island maps; signposts on the ground often show place names rather than route numbers.

Samui's road network

Almost everything on Samui hangs off one loop. The ring road follows the coast at a distance of a few hundred metres to a couple of kilometres, so you reach most beaches by a short side road (a soi) from the main road. The interior is hilly and mostly forest and coconut plantation, crossed by a handful of steep concrete roads to waterfalls, viewpoints and hillside villas.

RoadSectionCharacterMain hazards
Route 4169 (ring road)Full loop: Chaweng, Bophut, Maenam, Nathon, Na Mueang, LamaiPaved, mostly two lanes, with frequent junctions and U-turn gapsTrucks and minivans, turning traffic, U-turns, scooters overtaking on both sides; the hill between Lamai and Chaweng
Route 4170South-west: Lipa Noi, Thong Krut, Taling NgamNarrow, steep, short sharp gradients, blind bendsSand on the tarmac, slippery within minutes of rain, single-lane corners
Route 4171North-east: Bangrak, Plai Laem, Choeng Mon, Big Buddha causewayTwo lanes, busier near the piersPier and airport traffic, tour minivans, pedestrians at Big Buddha
Chaweng Beach RoadParallel to the beach, north to south through ChawengNarrow one-way sections, shops on both sidesTaxis stopping without warning, drunk pedestrians at night, crowds in the evening
Hill and villa roadsNa Muang, the Secret Buddha Garden road, Chaweng Noi and Bophut hillsSteep concrete, often unlitBrake fade on descents, wet algae, loose gravel

The round-island drive

Driving the whole loop is a classic day out. Non-stop it takes about 90 minutes; with a swim, lunch and three or four sights it fills a full day. Going clockwise from Chaweng keeps the sea on your left for most of the way, which makes it easier to pull in at viewpoints and beach car parks.

  1. Chaweng Start early, before the traffic builds. Take Route 4171 to the Big Buddha and Wat Plai Laem, then rejoin the ring road.
  2. Bophut A coffee stop at Fisherman's Village; park on the main road, not in the narrow lanes.
  3. Maenam The long, quiet north coast; flat, straight and the easiest stretch of the loop.
  4. Nathon The island's old port and government town, with petrol stations, banks and the pier. See Nathon.
  5. Lipa Noi and Taling Ngam Take Route 4170 for the west-coast sunset beaches and the Pig Island pier at Thong Krut. This is the steepest part of the drive; fill up with fuel first.
  6. Na Mueang Back on the ring road: Na Muang Waterfall is a short turn inland, and Wat Khunaram sits right on the main road.
  7. Hua Thanon and Lamai The Muslim fishing village, then Hin Ta and Hin Yai at the south end of Lamai (car park about 30 THB).
  8. Lad Koh viewpoint On the hill back towards Chaweng Noi. Pull fully off the road, and stay off the rocks in big waves.

Petrol stations cluster in Nathon, Lamai and along the Chaweng strip and thin out in the south-west and inland, so fill up before Route 4170 or the Na Muang road. A 125 cc scooter uses roughly 50–80 THB of fuel for the whole loop.

Hill roads and steep villa driveways

Samui's interior rises to 635 m at Khao Pom, and many villas, viewpoints and waterfalls sit on concrete roads that would be closed to traffic in Europe. They cause a large share of visitor accidents.

  • Secret Buddha Garden: the road up is so steep and broken that we recommend a 4x4 or a tour rather than a scooter or small rental car. See Secret Buddha Garden.
  • Na Muang 2: the upper waterfall is a 20–40 minute steep climb on foot from the car park; don't try to ride further up than the parking area. See Na Muang 2.
  • Overlap Stone road: a very steep climb from Maret above Lamai; low gear all the way. See Overlap Stone.
  • Villa driveways: in Chaweng Noi, Bophut hills and Taling Ngam, driveways of 20–30% are common. Ask your villa before you arrive whether a small car or scooter can manage the access, especially in the rain.

How to drive the hills

  • Go down in a low gear and use engine braking. Riding the brakes all the way down overheats them, and brake fade on a long descent is a common cause of crashes.
  • On a scooter, use both brakes gently and never grab the front brake on wet concrete.
  • Don't stop half-way up a steep slope with a passenger: many automatic scooters can't restart. Let the passenger walk the last section.
  • Black or green patches on concrete are algae and as slippery as ice when wet.

Rules of the road

RuleWhat it means on Samui
Side of the roadDrive on the left; give way to traffic already on the ring road when you pull out of a soi
HelmetsCompulsory for the rider and every passenger on every road; fine up to 2,000 THB per person since 1 June 2025
LicenceYour home licence plus an International Driving Permit (IDP); for scooters both must show the motorcycle category
SeatbeltsRequired for the driver and passengers in cars
Drink-driving0.05% blood alcohol for most drivers; 0.02% for drivers under 20, provisional licence holders and anyone without a valid licence
PhonesNo handheld phone use while driving or riding
LightsHeadlights on at night; many local bikes have none, so assume you haven't been seen

Seatbelts became compulsory for all car passengers, not only those in front, from September 2022. [check]

The national speed limit for cars in municipal areas, which covers all of Samui, is 80 km/h, and 60 km/h for motorcycles. [check]

In practice, nobody needs to go fast on Samui: the ring road is full of junctions, and an average speed of 30–40 km/h is normal. Read our scooter rental guide for the IDP rules in detail, and the car rental guide if you prefer four wheels.

Police checkpoints and fines

Police checkpoints are a regular sight near Chaweng Lake Road, near the airport and at points along Route 4169. Officers wave scooters in, check helmets, licences and IDPs, and sometimes test for alcohol at night.

OffenceTypical fine (THB)
No helmet, rider or passengerUp to 2,000 per person
No licence or no valid IDPTypically 500–1,000
Drink-drivingCourt case, heavy fine, possible jail and licence suspension
  • Carry your licence, IDP and a copy of your passport photo page and entry stamp every time you ride.
  • Stay calm and polite. A ticket is either paid at the police station or on the spot against an official receipt; always ask for the receipt.
  • Paying the fine does not make riding without the right licence legal for the rest of your trip, and it does nothing for your insurance cover.

Our Koh Samui police stations guide explains where fines are paid and how to report an incident.

Traffic hotspots and times

  • Chaweng Beach Road, evenings: slow from about 18:00 until late, with taxis stopping anywhere and crowds spilling off the pavement. Walk or park outside the centre.
  • Chaweng to the airport and the Bangrak piers: busy at boat and flight times; allow extra time if you have a ferry or a flight to catch.
  • Fisherman's Village on Friday: the road through the village closes to traffic from about 16:30 for the walking street. Scooters left inside the closed area can be towed, with a release fee of 500 THB or more. See Fisherman's Village walking street.
  • The Lamai–Chaweng hill: a fast, curving section where overtaking on the bends is common; keep left and keep your speed down.
  • School times: roads near schools in Nathon, Lamai and Bophut get busy in the morning and mid-afternoon on weekdays. [check]

Rainy season and flooding

Samui's wet season runs from October to December and peaks in November, with around 445 mm of rain in an average November. The first minutes of a downpour lift oil and fine sand to the surface, and the island's drains can't cope with tropical cloudbursts.

  • Flood-prone areas: low points on inland roads and the south-west back roads can flood in heavy rain from October to December. Water across the road often hides potholes and broken drain covers.
  • Sand on bends: after heavy rain, sand washes onto the road at corners near beaches and building sites.
  • Potholes: they appear quickly in the rainy season and are repaired slowly.
  • What to do: if you can't see the road surface under the water, turn back. Wait out heavy showers; most pass within an hour.

Check the forecast on our Koh Samui weather page or on Windy before a long ride. Current conditions: [kp_weather_now]. Official warnings come from the Thai Meteorological Department. Our November guide covers the wettest month in detail.

Parking and towing

  • Kerb colours: red and white means no stopping; yellow and white means no parking. Unmarked kerbs are usually tolerated, except where signs say otherwise.
  • Chaweng and Lamai: park scooters in marked bays or in front of the shop you are visiting, with permission. Cars are easier in mall and supermarket car parks.
  • Beach and sight car parks: often free; a few charge a small fee, such as about 30 THB at Hin Ta and Hin Yai and 20–60 THB at Na Muang.
  • Fisherman's Village: park on the ring road side on Fridays; don't leave a bike in the walking-street zone after about 16:30.
  • Security: lock the steering, take the key and never leave a helmet, phone or bag in the scooter basket.

If you crash

  1. Make the scene safe and move out of the traffic if you can do so without making injuries worse.
  2. Call for help: 1669 for an ambulance, 191 for the police or 1155 for the English-speaking Tourist Police.
  3. Take photos of the vehicles, their number plates, the road and any injuries, and swap phone numbers with the other party.
  4. Call your rental shop and your travel insurer's emergency line, ideally before major treatment.
  5. Get a police report. Your insurer will want it. The police station covering the area where the crash happened makes the report; the Tourist Police can help with language.
  6. Don't sign anything you can't read. Ask for an English translation or for the Tourist Police to explain a document before you sign it.
  7. Don't hand over your passport as a guarantee to a rental shop or the other party.

Private hospitals with 24-hour emergency departments are in Chaweng and Bophut; see Koh Samui hospitals. For disputes after a minor crash, the Tourist Police can mediate.

Are Samui's roads dangerous?

Honestly, yes, compared with home. The UK government notes that Thailand has a high number of road accidents, particularly involving motorcycles, and the WHO ranks it among the world's deadliest countries for motorcycle deaths. On Samui the pattern is familiar to every hospital: visitors who rarely ride at home, a hired scooter, a wet hill or a late night, and no helmet. The risk falls sharply if you wear a helmet, ride sober, stay off the hills in the rain and avoid riding after dark.

If you don't ride confidently at home, don't learn here. Use Grab, taxis or a driver (see getting around Koh Samui), hire a private van with driver from 2,500 THB for 4 hours, or see the hill sights on the Jungle Discovery jeep safari (1,500 THB adult). The sea is the easier way to explore: the Pig Island speedboat tour (1,450 THB adult) runs all year with hotel pickup from most areas of Koh Samui, and the Ang Thong big boat tour (1,500 THB adult) runs again from 16 December, when the marine park reopens after its 1 November–15 December closure.
